title: The SIMT Execution Model
summary: Warps, lockstep threads, and the divergence penalty that makes GPU branching fundamentally different from CPU branching.

slides.markdown:
**SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads)** is the GPU's execution model: many threads execute the *same instruction* at the *same time*, each on its own private data. Every thread has its own registers and program counter conceptually, but the hardware issues one instruction to a whole group of them per cycle.

This is why a GPU kernel is written as if it were a single thread's logic — `"compute this pixel"` — and then launched millions of times. The SIMT model is what lets one instruction fetch/decode serve dozens of ALU lanes at once, which is exactly the control-logic saving that makes GPU throughput possible ([gpu-architecture-fundamentals](gpu-architecture-fundamentals)).

A **warp** (NVIDIA's term; AMD calls it a **wavefront**) is the actual group of threads — typically 32 — that the hardware schedules and moves together in lockstep. You can *write* a kernel for one logical thread, but the scheduler never runs fewer than a full warp at a time.

This matters because a warp is the true unit of execution: if even one thread in a warp needs to do work, the whole warp occupies a lane. An oddly-sized problem (say, 33 elements) still consumes two full warps, wasting most of the second one — a rounding cost every GPU programmer eventually has to account for.

A warp maps cleanly onto hardware: one instruction fetched and decoded once, then broadcast to every ALU lane in the warp, each lane pulling its own operands.

![A warp of 32 threads executing one shared instruction, each thread's data flowing into its own ALU lane](assets/warp-lockstep-execution.svg)

That single fetch/decode serving 32 lanes is the direct payoff of SIMT — it's why GPUs can dedicate so much more silicon to ALUs than a CPU ([gpu-architecture-fundamentals](gpu-architecture-fundamentals)) rather than repeating control logic per lane.

assets.alt: A warp of 32 threads executing one shared instruction, each thread's data flowing into its own ALU lane

slides.markdown:
**Branch divergence** happens when threads within the same warp disagree on a branch — say, `if (x[i] > 0)` is true for some threads and false for others. Because a warp can only execute *one* instruction stream at a time, the hardware runs **both paths sequentially**, masking off the threads that don't take each path.

Threads on the "wrong" path for a given pass simply do nothing (their results are discarded), but they still occupy a lane and burn a cycle. A warp with a divergent branch effectively pays the **sum** of both branches' costs instead of the cost of just one — parallelism you thought you had quietly disappears.

SIMT is often confused with **SIMD**, but they're different mechanisms for the same idea (apply one operation across data).

| | SIMD | SIMT |
|---|---|---|
| Programming view | One thread, wide vector registers | Many threads, each scalar-looking |
| Divergence handling | No native branching per lane | Masks divergent paths per warp |
| Where it lives | CPU vector units (see [simd-and-vector-processing](simd-and-vector-processing)) | GPU warps/wavefronts |

SIMD asks a programmer to explicitly pack data into vectors; SIMT lets each thread look independent while the hardware secretly runs them in lockstep — which is why divergence is a SIMT-specific cost that SIMD code doesn't experience the same way.

A common mistake porting CPU code to a GPU is writing kernels with heavy **per-thread branching** — a big `switch` or nested `if/else` where neighboring threads take genuinely different paths based on their data.

On a CPU, branch prediction handles this cheaply per core. On a GPU, if threads within a warp diverge, the warp serializes every distinct path taken, and the promised 32x-wide parallelism can collapse toward 1x for that warp. The fix isn't "never branch" — it's structuring data so threads *within a warp* tend to take the same path (e.g., sorting or grouping by branch condition before launching the kernel).
